outputs.L1:
They thought the field was going to waste, so they gathered the marker rocks and stones and piled them in a barn. They say the rocks were shaped, some scratched with triangles and other forms. They must have been trying to invent some new language. They say the rocks were used to build that wall there, guarding the manor, and a few were used for the state house. Crops refused to grow.

I say the stones marked an old tongue, and it was called eternity, and it pointed toward the river. I say that, after that collection, no pillow in the big house dreamed. I say that somewhere beneath here moulders one called Alice, whose great-grandson is old now, too, and refuses to talk about slavery. I say that, at the master’s table, only one plate is set for supper. I say no seed can flourish on this ground, once planted and then forsaken. Wild berries warm a field of bones. Bloom how you must, I say.
outputs.L2:
Believing the land was going to ruin, they collected its marker stones and carried them into a barn, stacking them there. Some say those rocks had been carved—certain ones scored with triangles, others with different shapes—as though someone had been creating an unfamiliar language. They say the stones were later used in the wall over there that protects the manor, with a small number going into the state house.

Nothing would grow afterward.

I say those markings belonged to an ancient speech called eternity, and that they directed the way to the river. I say that once the stones were removed, not a single pillow in the great house held a dream. Beneath this place, somewhere, decays a woman named Alice. Her great-grandson has grown old as well, and he will not speak of slavery.

I say the master’s supper table is laid with only one plate. No seed will thrive in soil that was first cultivated and then abandoned. Wild berries ripen above a field filled with bones.

Bloom however you are able, I say.
outputs.L3:
Believing that the field had failed and would never again produce a useful harvest, people began removing the marked stones embedded in its soil. They treated the stones as ordinary building material, carrying them away to construct a barn, a wall around the manor, and even part of the state house. Yet the stones were not unmarked or meaningless. Scratched across their surfaces were triangles and other shapes that may once have formed an ancient language—a system of signs directing those who could read it toward the river.

Once the stones were gone, the land seemed to change. Crops would no longer grow in the disturbed field, and the manor built from its materials became haunted by a pervasive sense of loss and absence. What had been displaced could not be restored, and what had been buried could not remain entirely silent.

Beneath the ground lie the remains of people such as Alice, whose life is entangled with the history of slavery. Her descendants refuse to speak about that past, leaving her story unacknowledged and the buried history of the land unresolved. The field was planted, exhausted, and finally forsaken, but it was never truly empty. Wild berries still bloom there, spreading their roots and bright fruit over a field of bones.
outputs.L4:
The old people said that the stones had once stood upright in the field, each one planted with purpose. Their faces were cut with signs no one living could fully read—perhaps fragments of an ancestral language, perhaps names, prayers, or directions. Some leaned toward the river as though pointing the way to water, escape, or home. Others marked the resting places of those who had labored and died there.

When the manor was enlarged, the stones were pulled from the earth. Wagons carried them away to be fitted into the manor wall and, later, into the foundations of the state house. What had preserved the dead was made to support the power of those who wished them forgotten. The graves disappeared beneath plows and roads, and the inscriptions were turned inward, hidden by mortar. With the stones removed, even memory lost its landmarks. The history of slavery could be denied because the ground had been stripped of its witnesses.

Nothing prospered in that field afterward. The soil lay thin and barren, and the place seemed abandoned even when people crossed it. At night it felt inhabited by an unseen company, as if the dead still waited for their names to be spoken. Only the wild berries returned each year, flowering among the weeds and spreading their dark fruit over the neglected earth. Beneath them, scattered through the field, remained the bones.
outputs.L5:
### They Thought the World Was Ending

They thought the storm would pass before morning. They thought the river would remain behind its banks, the old bridge would hold, and the lights in every house would stay on.

They thought the warnings were exaggerated.

But when the rain grew heavier and the streets disappeared beneath dark water, certainty gave way to silence. Neighbors who had barely spoken began knocking on one another’s doors. They carried children, shared food, rescued pets, and guided the elderly toward higher ground.

By sunrise, the storm had taken fences, cars, and pieces of the bridge. Yet it had also revealed something they had forgotten: a community was not made of roads or buildings, but of people willing to help one another.

They thought the disaster would destroy them. Instead, it reminded them how to stand together.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a haunting prose poem in the voice of an ancestral witness describing a former plantation where grave markers were removed, repurposed into walls and buildings, and the buried enslaved remain forgotten beneath barren ground.
counterfactuals.output:
I was here before the house learned to call itself historic.

I watched them lower my children into the earth without stone or psalm, each grave marked by what the living could spare: a river rock, a cedar stake, a shard of crockery pressed into clay. At night we spoke the names again, so the dark would not swallow them whole. Ama. Ben. Little Ruth. Isaac, who carried the scar of an iron ring. We made a country of memory beneath the pines.

Years passed. The fields went pale. The columns were washed white enough to pretend innocence.

Then men came with wagons and prybars. They lifted the markers from our dead as if gathering loose teeth. Some stones were mortared into a garden wall. Some became steps for the kitchen door, thresholds polished by generations of unknowing shoes. One bears the ghost of a letter beneath limewash. Another holds up the corner of a building where visitors sip sweet tea and admire the old workmanship.

No one asks what the stones once guarded.

The ground where we were buried has been scraped clean. No grass takes there. In summer it hardens and splits; in winter, rain gathers in the hollows where bodies settled. They call it an empty field. They say nothing is there.

But I am there.

I move under the barren earth with all who were denied an ending. We remember the weight of cotton sacks, the bell before dawn, the names given and the names kept hidden behind the teeth. We remember births by firelight, hands clasped in cane breaks, songs carried low so sorrow would not hear itself and die.

Sometimes a child leans against the garden wall and feels it shiver. Sometimes a guest pauses on the threshold, troubled by a cold no weather made. Sometimes, near evening, the buildings groan though there is no wind.

That is not age.

That is the dead pressing their names back through the stone.

Listen: every wall is speaking. Every step is a mouth. Beneath the field, the forgotten lie shoulder to shoulder, holding the plantation above them like a terrible dream.

We do not ask to haunt this place.

We ask to be found.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental, punctuation-free monologue about slavery, erased history, and stones carved with mysterious symbols, repeating the phrase “i say” throughout.
counterfactuals.output:
i say the stones remember what the books refused to hold

i say beneath the moss there are names without graves

i say beneath the names there are hands still reaching through the earth

i say slavery was not silence

i say silence was built around it

i say every erased page leaves a white wound

i say the archive closes its mouth while the river keeps speaking

i say the stones are carved with spirals suns broken ladders and eyes

i say no one living knows who cut them

i say someone living still profits from forgetting

i say the symbols tremble when rain enters their grooves

i say they might be maps

i say they might be warnings

i say they might be the last alphabet of those forbidden to write

i say listen with your palm

i say feel how the cold surface becomes a door

i say on the other side iron drags across morning

i say on the other side a mother hides a true name inside a song

i say on the other side the dead refuse the names their owners gave them

i say history calls itself complete

i say history is a room with missing walls

i say the stones stand where witnesses were buried

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Southern Gothic poem in which a field refuses to grow after people gather its marked rocks into a barn, unaware that they have disturbed an old burial ground.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Field Keeps Its Dead**

Come April, nothing took the rain—  
not corn, not cane, not bitter rye.  
The field lay flat beneath the crows,  
a shut and yellow eye.

All winter long, the Mercer boys  
had cleared the stones for planting,  
each one scratched with crooked marks  
they took for weather’s writing.

They hauled them to the leaning barn  
and stacked them by the stalls,  
where moonlight made the markings stir  
like briars on the walls.

Then cattle shied from empty air,  
and milk went black by dawn.  
At night, the hayloft whispered names  
of Mercers dead and gone.

The old field drank each thunderstorm  
and gave no blade, no weed—  
only pale hands of fungus raised  
where furrows waited seed.

Miss Ada from the cypress road  
came limping through the mud.  
She touched one stone and crossed herself.  
“That ain’t no farmer’s scrawl,” she said.

“Those marks are prayers the earth once kept.  
Those rocks were set for bones.”  
Behind her, all the barn doors slammed,  
though wind had left them lone.

They carried every marker back  
beneath a blistered sun,  
but none could say which grave was whose  
or where the rows had run.

So still they lie, misplaced, unnamed,  
while roots recoil below;  
and every spring the Mercers plant—

but the field  
refuses  
to grow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical historical piece narrated by the land itself, connecting displaced gravestones, an abandoned manor, a woman named Alice, inherited silence about slavery, and wild berries blooming over bones.
counterfactuals.output:
I remember where every stone was first set.

Before the road was widened, before the cedar roots shouldered through the burial ground, the markers stood in a crooked congregation above the river. Some bore names cut deep enough to hold rain. Others had only initials, or a lamb, or a hand pointing toward a heaven their makers believed was elsewhere.

Then men came with wagons and iron bars. They lifted the gravestones and carried them uphill, arranging them neatly beside the church. They called it preservation. Beneath the old hill, the graves remained.

I held my dead without complaint.

The manor watched from its rise, all columns and shuttered eyes. Once, its windows flashed with candlelight. Once, horses stamped in the yard, and bells rang from the kitchen to summon hands whose names were not entered in the family Bible. The house recorded births, marriages, silver spoons, acres of wheat. It did not record every child sold south, every woman made to nurse another woman’s baby, every man buried at the edge of the orchard after dark.

But I recorded them.

Their heels pressed paths into me. Their hoes opened my red clay. Their sweat salted my furrows. Blood entered me too, and tears, and the small lost things that fall from pockets: a blue bead, a bent button, a coin worn smooth by wishing.

Alice found the bead one summer after the war had become a bronze plaque in town.

She was nine, barefoot, and forbidden to enter the ruined manor. By then, ivy had climbed through the dining-room windows, rain had softened the stairs, and foxes slept beneath the library floor. Alice went anyway. Children understand that a prohibition is often a door left ajar.

Her family had owned the land for generations. That was the sentence repeated at Sunday tables, polished like the mahogany no one could afford to repair. Owned the land. No one said who had worked it. No one said whom else they had owned.

When Alice asked about the cabins sunk beyond the pines, her grandmother folded a napkin into smaller and smaller squares.

“That was long ago,” she said.

Silence is also an inheritance. It passes from mouth to mouth, lighter than silver and harder to surrender.

Alice carried it for years.

She left, married, buried her mother, returned. The manor had lost part of its roof. In the family cemetery uphill, the displaced stones leaned in tidy rows, honoring empty ground. Alice walked among them reading her own bloodline: colonels, judges, faithful wives. At the bottom of the hill, where the original graves lay unmarked, blackberry canes had taken hold.

They flowered white over the bones.

In June the blossoms shone like little witnesses. In August the fruit darkened—purple, then black—each berry made of many chambers, each chamber holding a seed.

Alice ate one. Its sweetness broke against her tongue, followed by the faint taste of iron.

That year she opened the ledgers in the courthouse. She read inventories where people appeared between cattle and bedsteads. She found an Alice listed there too: female, nineteen, seamstress, value eight hundred dollars.

For a long while, the living Alice rested her hand on the paper.

I had known both their footsteps.

She began to speak the names she could recover. At first alone, then to cousins who objected, then to schoolchildren beneath the collapsing portico. She told them the manor had not been abandoned when the family departed. It had been abandoned much earlier—each time a truth was omitted, each time suffering was renamed custom, each time wealth was praised without naming its cost.

Some listened. Some turned away. The house continued falling.

Houses do that. So do empires. Stone splits. Timber bows. Paper browns at the edges. Even lies require maintenance.

I remain.

Under the blackberries, the dead lie where they were placed. Above them, the gravestones keep their mistaken vigil on the hill. Alice is old now. She comes in late summer with a basket and a walking stick. She leaves the first berries untouched.

“For you,” she says.

The roots carry sweetness downward. Rain moves through carved names and nameless ribs alike. The manor gives another sigh and settles deeper into my grasses.

Do not mistake my silence for forgetting.

I am the field, the grave, the road, the foundation. I have borne every house and outlasted every claim. What is buried in me does not vanish. It changes form.

Bone becomes mineral. Iron becomes rust. Silence becomes story.

And over all of it, year after year, the wild berries bloom.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a stream-of-consciousness prose poem about archaeological erasure on a plantation, where carved stones are mistaken for debris and used to construct a manor wall and state house; end with the defiant image “bloom how you must i say.”
counterfactuals.output: They called the stones rubble because rubble does not accuse, because debris can be lifted without asking whose hands carved the crescent, the river, the small untranslatable wings; and so the wagons came through cane-shadow and cotton hush, iron rims grinding the road above the quarters, carrying names no ledger had bothered to keep. In the manor wall the stones learned a new grammar: chimney, lintel, wealth. Mortar covered their mouths, though rain kept finding the grooves. Later, more were pried from the burial slope and hauled to the state house, fitted beneath white columns where men declared history settled, property lawful, memory an inconvenience. I press my ear to the cool façade and hear the field breathing inside it, hear broken bowls, heel bones, buttons, seeds, the buried doorways of cabins, hear every carved mark refusing the word accidental. Vines enter wherever the builders failed to imagine a future. Roots lever apart the official sentences. A flower opens from the crack beside the cornerstone, red as a wound and ordinary as weather, and bloom how you must i say.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
